steps.markdown: A **random forest** trains many decision trees and averages their predictions (or takes a vote). Individual trees are noisy; their average is much more stable.

Two sources of randomness keep the trees different: each tree trains on a **bootstrap sample** (rows drawn with replacement, called **bagging**), and each split considers only a random subset of features.
Averaging many decorrelated trees mainly reduces **variance**, so forests overfit far less than single deep trees, usually with little tuning.

Bonus: each tree skips about a third of the rows, so those **out-of-bag** rows give a free validation estimate. Forests also report **feature importances**, though these can favor features with many possible split points.

steps.question: What does bagging mean?
choices: Training each model on a random sample of rows drawn with replacement
Training trees one after another on their mistakes
steps.explanation: Bootstrap aggregating: resample rows, train a model on each sample, aggregate.

steps.question: Random forests mainly improve on a single tree by reducing…
steps.explanation: Averaging many noisy but different trees cancels much of their variance.

steps.question: Why consider only a random subset of features at each split?
choices: Because trees can't handle many features
To make each tree more accurate on its own
So the trees are less similar and their errors cancel out better
steps.explanation: Without it, every tree would pick the same strong features and make similar mistakes.
